title: Understanding Your Annual Pay: Hourly Rates, Salary Protection Insurance, and Tax Estimates
description: Convert your hourly rate to annual salary with our guide. Includes salary protection insurance, tax brackets, superannuation, and award rates for Australian workers.
salarySummary: For a 38-hour week, annual gross pay is hourly rate multiplied by 38 then by 52, with super paid on top.

faqs.q: How is annual salary calculated from hourly rate?
faqs.a: Annual gross pay is calculated as hourly rate × hours per week × 52. For a standard full-time role of 38 hours, that's hourly × 38 × 52. This assumes the same rate every week with no unpaid overtime, penalty rates, or allowances. The result is a gross figure before tax and super.

faqs.q: What is the difference between the National Minimum Wage and award rates?
faqs.a: The National Minimum Wage is the legal floor set by the Fair Work Commission, currently $26.44 per hour from 1 July 2026. Award rates are higher minimums for specific industries or occupations, set by the Fair Work Ombudsman. Many workers are covered by an award that pays above the national minimum. Casual employees also receive a 25% loading on top of the base rate.

faqs.q: How does salary protection insurance relate to my pay?
faqs.a: Salary protection insurance (also called income protection) replaces a portion of your income if you cannot work due to illness or injury. It is typically offered through superannuation funds or purchased separately. The premium is often a percentage of your insured salary, so understanding your annual pay helps you choose appropriate cover.

bodyMarkdown:
## Converting Your Hourly Rate to Annual Pay

When you know your hourly rate, the simplest way to estimate your annual gross pay is to multiply that rate by the number of hours you work each week, then by 52 weeks. For a standard full-time role of 38 hours per week, the formula is:

**Annual gross ≈ hourly rate × 38 × 52**

This gives you a figure that assumes the same rate every week, with no unpaid overtime, penalty rates, allowances, or salary sacrifice. It is a starting point for budgeting, tax planning, and considering salary protection insurance.

### The Fortnightly View

Many Australians are paid fortnightly. Your fortnightly gross pay is simply your weekly pay multiplied by two. For a 38-hour week, that is:

**Fortnightly gross = hourly rate × 38 × 2**

Knowing your fortnightly amount helps you match your budget to your pay cycle and compare with salary offers that are quoted per annum.

## National Minimum Wage vs. Award Rates

The Fair Work Commission sets the National Minimum Wage, which from 1 July 2026 is $26.44 per hour, or $1,004.90 per week for 38 hours. This is the legal minimum for employees not covered by an award or registered agreement. However, most workers are covered by an industry or occupation award that sets higher minimum rates. The Fair Work Ombudsman publishes pay guides for each award.

### Casual Loading

Casual employees receive a 25% loading on top of the base hourly rate to compensate for not receiving paid leave. For the National Minimum Wage, the casual rate is $33.05 per hour. If you are casual, remember that the loading is added to the base rate, not included in it. Our [timesheet](/) includes a checkbox to add 25% casual loading automatically.

## Superannuation Paid on Top

Employers must pay superannuation guarantee contributions of 12% of your ordinary earnings, on top of your gross pay. This is not deducted from your hourly rate; it is an additional cost to your employer. The super guarantee applies up to a maximum contribution base of $270,830 per year (2026–27). For most full-time workers, super is calculated on your ordinary time earnings, which for a 38-hour week is your hourly rate × 38.

When estimating your total remuneration package, include super. For example, if your hourly rate is $40, your annual gross pay is $40 × 38 × 52 = $79,040. Your employer would also contribute $9,484.80 in super (12% of $79,040), making your total package $88,524.80. See our [super and packaging](/topics/super-and-packaging) page for more details.

## Tax Estimates for 2026–27

The Australian Taxation Office applies a progressive tax scale for residents in 2026–27:

- Nil tax on the first $18,200
- 15% on income from $18,201 to $45,000
- 30% on income from $45,001 to $135,000
- 37% on income from $135,001 to $190,000
- 45% on income above $190,000

In addition, most residents pay a Medicare levy of 2% of taxable income. The 2025–26 single reduction thresholds are used here because the 2026–27 thresholds were not confirmed. This estimate does not include the Medicare levy surcharge, HELP repayments, or salary packaging.

For a worker earning $79,040 per year, the tax would be approximately:
- $0 on first $18,200
- 15% on $26,800 ($18,201 to $45,000) = $4,020
- 30% on $34,040 ($45,001 to $79,040) = $10,212
- Total tax = $14,232
- Medicare levy (2%) = $1,580.80
- Total deductions = $15,812.80
- Net annual pay ≈ $63,227.20

This is a rough guide. Use our [take-home pay](/topics/take-home) page for a more detailed calculator.

## Industry Averages vs. Job Medians

The Australian Bureau of Statistics publishes Average Weekly Earnings (AWE) data. For May 2026, full-time adult ordinary time earnings averaged $2,083.70 per week, or about $108,352 per year. All employees (including part-time) averaged $1,579.20 per week. These are averages across all industries, not medians for a specific job.

For example, the financial and insurance services industry had average full-time ordinary time earnings of $2,341.30 per week in May 2026. This is an industry average, not the median pay for a particular role like a bank teller or financial analyst. Job-specific medians are not provided here; refer to our [job pay](/topics/job-pay) page for more context.

## Why Consider Salary Protection Insurance?

Salary protection insurance (also called income protection) is designed to replace a portion of your income if you cannot work due to illness or injury. Understanding your annual pay is essential when choosing a cover amount. Typically, policies cover up to 75% of your gross income, including super contributions. The premium is often a percentage of the insured amount, so knowing your annual gross pay helps you budget for the cost.

Many superannuation funds offer group salary protection insurance, which may be cheaper than a retail policy. However, the terms and conditions vary. Always check the product disclosure statement. For more on how super and insurance interact, see our [super and packaging](/topics/super-and-packaging) page.

## Important Disclaimer

The annual pay shown here is an estimate based on hourly rate × hours per week × 52. It assumes the same rate every week, no unpaid overtime, no penalty rates, no allowances, and no salary sacrifice. Super is estimated at 12% of ordinary earnings only, paid on top, and stops at the $270,830 maximum contribution base. Tax uses the 2026–27 resident scale with the full tax-free threshold. Medicare uses the 2025–26 single reduction thresholds because the 2026–27 reduction thresholds were not confirmed here. HELP, the Medicare levy surcharge, and salary packaging are not deducted. This is an estimate, not a determination of your pay or tax.

For a more precise calculation, use our [reference tables](/data) or consult a qualified accountant.
